fin_reserve.label: Build a cash reserve
case: I want three weeks of running costs sitting in the float. Costs are {expenses} a week and the float is {float}, so we're on {weeks} weeks. With three, a late payer doesn't scare me, and I can say yes when someone needs a hand.

Let's get the float up to three weeks of costs. Running costs are {expenses} a week, the float is {float}, which is {weeks} weeks. I'm tired of working out which bill waits. Cover the bills and the spare is ours to spend on people who need it.

The target is three weeks of costs held back. We spend {expenses} a week and hold {float}, so that's {weeks} weeks. One slow week shouldn't be a crisis. With that cushion I can sell when the price is right, not when I'm desperate.

I'd like three weeks of costs in the float. Costs are {expenses} a week, float is {float}, so {weeks} weeks. Short of that, one bad week and we're begging. Past it, we can lend a few quid to someone who's short and not feel it.

craft_first.label: Craft more {calc}
case: I'd rather we craft 30% of the {calc} made in London. We're on {share}%. The Guild still sets the standard for a good piece. The more we make, the more buyers set ours beside theirs. I'm not worried about that comparison.

Let's craft 30% of London's {calc}. Our share is {share}%, and {rival} makes the most besides us. Buyers can only judge our work if they see plenty of it. More of it on the market means more of them comparing it with the Guild's.

Aim for 30% of the {calc} crafted in London. You're on {share}%. Raw ore sells on price alone, and I don't like that. Crafted {calc} sells on quality, which is where we beat the Guild, so I want more of it out there.

The target is 30% of London's crafted {calc}. At present it's {share}%. The Guild's work is the standard buyers know. Every piece of ours they see is a chance to show we're better, and {rival} isn't taking that chance.

craft_rankup.label: Better work at the bench
case: Take one recipe you already know and push it past your best rank. I'd like at least one recipe higher than it stands today, two if you can manage. A higher rank means a better piece, and a better piece is what lets us name a price the Guild can't undercut.

Raise a recipe's rank this week, any recipe. Two would be better. The firm is only as good as its best bench work. Higher rank means better pieces, and better pieces are how we show the Guild's standard isn't the ceiling.

I want at least one recipe ranked up by Sunday, and two if the ore allows. Same recipe, finer result. Buyers pay for quality they can see, and the Guild has relied on them not looking closely at ours.

Rank up a recipe, then another. It's the one thing here that doesn't depend on the market. A higher rank makes a better piece, a better piece sells for more, and I'd like to meet the Guild's standard from above.

craft_master.label: Master a recipe
case: I want a recipe at rank five. You have recipes at rank three or better, so the last two ranks are the only gap. Rank five is the best a piece can be made, and a firm that has one can fairly say it's passed the Guild's standard, not met it.

Master a recipe, take it to rank five. Two, if you can. You've already got work at rank three or above, so you know the cost of those last steps. A mastered recipe gives us pieces the Guild's own benches can't beat, and I'd like that on the record.

Bring one recipe to rank five this week. It's the top of the scale. Mastery is what lets us say we're better than the Guild and have a bench to prove it. You're close enough that it would be a waste to stop at three.

Take a recipe to rank five. We have work at rank three or better, so this is finishing, not starting. The Guild calls its masters a standard. I'd like us to be the standard, and one mastered recipe is the proof.

share_first.label: A slice of {calc}
case: I want 25% of London's {calc} this week. You're on {share}%. While we're small, any firm that cuts its price drags ours down with it. At 25% we start moving the price ourselves. James says the contested ore right now is {contested}.

Let's take a quarter of the {calc} market. We're on {share}%. Right now other firms' price swings decide our week. A quarter and we stop being pushed around by them. James's note: the factions are scrapping over {contested}.

Aim for 25% of London's {calc}. We hold {share}%. A bigger share means a steadier price, and a steadier price means I can pay the bills without checking the market first. James says {contested} is the contested ore at the moment.

A quarter of London's {calc}, that's the ask. You're at {share}%. Once we're that size, the price swings are partly ours, and spare cash gets easier to find for people who need it. James reckons {contested} is where the fighting is.

share_higher.label: Push {calc} higher
case: Let's take {calc} up to 40%. We're on {share}%, and the biggest other seller is {rival}. At that size we stop reacting to other firms' price drops and start causing them. That's the security I want for the bills.

I want 40% of London's {calc}. You're on {share}% and {rival} is the next biggest. A firm that size sets the price and the others follow. I'd rather follow nobody. Steadier income means more spare for people who need it.
Push {calc} to 40%. We're at {share}% and {rival} is the one we'd be taking it from. Right now their price swings land on us. At 40% it works the other way round, and I sleep better.
The next step is 40% of {calc}. You're on {share}%, {rival} is next down. Once we're big enough, a price swing is something we cause. That's worth more to me than the extra sales.

share_leader.label: Lead the {calc} market
case: I want us the biggest seller of {calc} in London, 35% at least. You're on {share}% and {rival} is the one to beat. The biggest seller sets the price and everyone else follows. I'd rather set it than follow it.
Take first place on {calc}, with a 35% share. We're at {share}% and {rival} is in the way. The top seller doesn't get pushed around by anyone's price swing. That's the security I want.

Be the largest seller of {calc}, at 35% or better. You're on {share}%, and {rival} is the biggest other name. First place means the price is partly ours to move, and we'll have more spare to give away.
First place on {calc}: 35% and the biggest share in town. You hold {share}%. {rival} sits just behind. Whoever leads decides what the market does, so I'd like it to be us, not them.

share_leader_james.label: Lead the {calc} market
case: I want us the leading seller of {calc} in London, at 35% or better. We're on {share}%, and {rival} is the one to pass. The Guild's standard for a leading house is the biggest share of an ore. Meeting it is the least I'll accept.
Take first place on {calc}, at a 35% share. You hold {share}% and {rival} is ahead. A house that leads its ore is one the Guild has to deal with as an equal. Then they can't say we're beneath them.

Be the largest seller of {calc}, with 35% or more. You're at {share}%, and {rival} is the name above yours. First place is how the Guild measures a house. I'd like the measure to come out in our favour for once.

First place on {calc}, 35% at least. Your share is {share}% and {rival} stands in the way. The Guild counts a house that leads its ore as a real one. Sell more {calc} than anyone and it has to count us.

share_second.label: Second ore: {calc}
case: Let's take 25% of {calc} as well. You're at {share}%. One ore means one bad price week can sink us. A second one means a swing in one is covered by the other. That's bills paid without panic.
I want a second ore, {calc}, at 25% of London's supply. You hold {share}%. With two lines, one bad week doesn't take everything. Steady money is what lets me help people out.
Get {calc} up to 25%. You're on {share}% now. If all our income rides on one ore, other firms' price swings decide our week. Two ores and they only decide half of it.
A second ore: 25% of {calc}. We're at {share}%. It's small now, which is the point. It's cheap to grow while nobody's watching, and it means we're not leaning on one price to pay the bills.

cult_yield.label: A bit more yield
case: If the veins gave a bit more than usual this week... only if that's all right. Your last ten days give a baseline, and a bit past it is the ask. Nothing heroic.
I've been watching the numbers. Not in a weird way. They could go up a little, I think. If we asked nicely. I averaged the last ten days. Twice. A bit above that is the whole plan.
Could we try for a bit past our usual? Just a bit. I've written the number down and then crossed it out. The ten-day average is the number to beat. Gently. Veins respond to gentle.

I had an idea about the yield. It's a small idea. I'll go first, so it's quicker if it's bad. Ten days of yield, averaged, is the line. I'd like us a little over it, and I'd like someone to tell me if that's daft.

cult_new_vein.label: Bring a vein online
case: There's a new vein that could come good. I could watch it. If you'd like. A fresh vein only counts once it's healthy enough to work. That's the bit I'd be watching.
There's one in the files nobody's looked at since you got it. I looked at it. It looked back, a bit. It has to get healthy first, then it counts. I'd check on it every morning, if that's allowed.
I'd like to try bringing a new vein up. I've read about it. I've read about it a lot. You've got a vein that isn't earning yet. Get it to working health and it's a new line on the sheet.
Archie says I should aim higher. This is higher. It's one vein higher. A vein that's only on paper doesn't count. A vein that's well enough to work does. I'd like the second kind.

cult_health_streak.label: Keep a vein healthy
case: A vein held in good condition night after night. Nobody's tried it properly. The nightly count only runs while a vein stays in good shape. One slip and it starts over.
I'd like to keep one vein well. Every night. I'll stay late, I don't mind. I've brought a flask. It's counted every night, and a bad night resets it. I know. I've thought about the bad night a lot.
It's not a big ask, it's a long one. A vein, kept in good shape, for days on the trot. A vein has to stay in good shape for the whole run of nights. The count doesn't forgive. I would.
What if one vein just... never had a bad night? I can't stop thinking about it. Each night it holds, the count goes up one. Each night it doesn't, it's back to nothing. I did warn you it was small.

cult_second_ore.label: A second ore
case: Not to alarm anyone, but we only have one kind of calc. Could we have two? Two ore types in good health means the business isn't one bad week from empty.
I keep thinking about the other kinds of calc. We don't have any. I keep thinking about that. If one ore has a bad week, the other doesn't. That's the whole argument. It's not a long one.
Could we grow a second sort of calc? I'll do the reading. I've already done the reading. A second ore, healthy enough to work, and the books stop leaning on one vein for everything.

James says one thing done well is a craft. Archie says one thing is a risk. Could I have a second thing? Both ores have to be in good shape for it to count. Two is steadier than one. I checked with the biscuits and it holds.

meeting._comment: Monday meeting (BoardMeetings.meeting_context()). Text is placeholder copy; PROSE-REVIEW: every string here is new.
meeting.minutesNone: No goal on the books last week.

minutes._comment: Minutes reaction (BoardMeetings.minutes_line()). groups maps a history result to a reaction group; variant = entry week mod list size. Tokens: {label}, {tier}. skipped = the goal Archie picked for you (tuning.skipVoice). PROSE-REVIEW: all new copy.

full: Archie reads it off his phone. "{label}, {tier}. Don't make that face. It's a good number."
Archie holds the phone up like a receipt. "{label}, {tier}. Somebody frame that."
base: "{label}. Base." Archie nods slowly. "A pass. Barely. I'm putting 'barely' in the minutes."
"{label}, base only." Archie taps the screen. "Door's open and you walked through it. Politely."
missed: "{label}, missed." Archie pockets the phone. "Next week, then."
"{label} didn't land." He says it like a cancelled bus. "There's another one in seven days."

full: James leans over Archie's phone. "{label}, {tier}. Competent." He straightens. "Minute that word, Archie. Exactly that word."
James reads the line, then reads it again. "{label}, {tier}. Archie has spelled 'reached' with two e's. I have corrected it. The result stands."
base: James takes his glasses off to read it. "{label}, base. Technically a pass. The minutes will say so. My opinion I will record separately."
"{label}, base only." James frowns at the screen. "Archie wrote 'solid'. I'd have written 'adequate'. We will settle on 'base'."
missed: "{label}, missed." James folds his arms. "It was a reasonable number. Next week it can be a reasonable number again."
James squints at the phone. "'Not reached', Archie, not 'failed'. They are different words and I will defend the difference. {label}, not reached."

full: Owen leans in, finger under the line. "{label}, {tier}. That's good, yeah? That's the good one?"
Owen reads it twice to be sure. "{label}, {tier}. I'd like that noted. Not by me. By someone."
base: "{label}, base." Owen nods like it's a bonus. "That's a pass. Passes count. I'm counting it."
Owen reads the line. "Base on {label}. It's the one before the good ones. I'm choosing to see it as the start of the good ones."
missed: Owen winces on your behalf. "{label}, missed. It's one week. I missed a whole year of dentist."
Owen holds the phone like it's warm. "{label}, missed. Next week, then. I'll bring biscuits."

full: "{label}, {tier}." Archie reads it out with great calm. "My pick, that was. I'll take the credit. You weren't using it."
"I picked {label}. We hit {tier}." Archie puts the phone down. "I'm only saying it the once."
base: "{label}, base. Mine, so I'm calling it a solid pass." He looks at you. "You'd have said the same."
"I picked {label} and it made base." Archie considers this. "Next time pick your own and I'll complain about that instead."
missed: "Mine, {label}. Missed." Archie doesn't dress it up. "Next week, then. Pick something yourself."
"I picked {label} and it didn't land." He says it flat, no excuse. "Happens. Put the kettle on."

aob._comment: Any other business (BoardMeetings.aob_line()): one seeded line per meeting, never the same as last week's. competing = used instead when two offered cards want the same ore; tokens {a}, {b} (pitchers), {ore}. Running gags: James and the minutes, Archie's catering, Owen's unasked questions, Archie poaching Owen. PROSE-REVIEW: all new copy.
competing: Archie notes that {a} and {b} both want {ore}. Nobody offers to share.
James observes that {a} and {b} have pitched for the same {ore}. He asks that the minutes call it a coincidence.
Owen asks whether {a} and {b} know they want the same {ore}. They do. It's why the room is quiet.
Archie says {a} and {b} can fight over {ore} in the car park. Not today, he adds. The car park is booked.
lines: James asks that the minutes record the date correctly this time. Archie says he has. James says he has seen the minutes.
James would like it noted that 'any other business' is not a catch-all for Archie's opinions. Archie asks that his objection be noted.
James reads back the last item. It's a different item from the one Archie wrote down. They agree to keep James's.
James spots a typo in the minutes and asks who typed it. Archie says autocorrect. James says autocorrect has never once written 'calk'.
Archie raises catering. There is no budget for catering. Archie says that is the problem.
Archie proposes catering, in the sense of a Greggs run. James asks that it be minuted as 'refreshments'.
Archie says next week there will be catering. He says it the way people say they'll start running.
Archie asks if the biscuits count as catering. Owen says they were his. Archie says that settles it.
Owen raises a hand and asks who gets the last biscuit. Nobody knew there was a question.
Owen asks whether the whiteboard counts as a vein. Nobody has an answer ready.
Owen asks what happens to the minutes after the meeting. James says they are filed. Owen asks where. James does not say.
Owen asks if this is the meeting where they decide things or the one where they talk about deciding. Archie says yes.
Archie tells Owen his offer still stands: better money, a van, and a desk with a drawer that locks. Owen says he'll think about the drawer.
Archie mentions, to nobody, that Owen would be wasted on a bench. Owen looks at the bench.
Archie slides a business card across to Owen. James slides it back. Neither of them says a word about it.
Archie offers Owen a lift home. Owen says he has a bus. Archie says buses are a choice.
Nobody has any other business. James asks that this be minuted. Archie asks that it be minuted as a miracle.
James raises the kettle. It's his, he'd like it back, and he'd like to know who has been descaling it with lemon.

meeting.agendaEmpty: Nobody has a pitch this week.

debate._comment: Debate scene (BoardMeetings.meeting_context()). PROSE-REVIEW: all copy is real prose (ticket 32). response[responder][pitcher][stance]: stances present are the ones the responder can take (Owen only wobbles); tokens {label}, {ore}. rebuttal plays only after a challenge, so it answers either challenger. clashOrder = voice pairs by how opposed their levers are; clash[pair] = list of 2-line exchanges [first voice, second voice]. chosen/concede tokens {label}.

james: The firm needs to be better than it is. That's the whole agenda, whatever the rest of you call it.
I'll be plain. We'll be judged on the work, and the work isn't good enough yet.
Whatever we choose this week, it should leave us ahead of the Guild's standard, not behind it.
archie: Right. What we need is money in the bank, so a bad week stops being a crisis.
Simple question: what gets us more cash and less worry? That's what I'm after.
Rent doesn't care how good our calc is. I want us comfortable first, then we can be proud.
owen: Um. Sorry. I think the business needs the veins to keep giving, and I can't see a good week without that.
I don't want to say the wrong thing. I think we need more coming out of the veins, and the rest follows.
Sorry, can I start? I think we should be sure of what we've got first. The veins, I mean.

back: Money buys us a better bench. I'll give you that, Archie.
A firm afraid of its bills makes rushed work. You're right about the cash.
Fine. If it stops us worrying about the rent, I can work in peace. I'll back it.
challenge: Selling more doesn't make it good. You're counting pounds, I'm counting quality.
Cash isn't standing, Archie. Buyers who only want the cheap one leave when someone is cheaper.
You keep saying safe. A safe firm that makes forgettable work is just closing slowly.

back: More from the veins means more on the bench. Sensible, Owen.
Yes. I can't craft what we haven't got. Carry on.
That, at least, I can find no fault with.
challenge: More of the same ore doesn't improve it, Owen. Yield without craft is a bigger pile.
Quantity is the easy part, Owen. What would we do with it?
That's what you always propose. Why is this week different?

back: Better work means we can ask more for it. I like that, James.
If it's good enough, buyers pay more. Fair enough.
Go on, then, make it better. Just make sure someone's buying it.
challenge: Lovely work, James. Does it sell? Rent's due either way.
Being proud of it doesn't pay the bills. Who's buying?
It's the Guild this and the Guild that every week. I'm trying to pay for things, not win an argument.

back: More from the veins is more to sell. Good call, Owen.
Can't argue with that. More stock, more sales, and nobody has to worry.
You picked a good one, Owen. I'll back it.
challenge: More stock's no use if it sits there, Owen. Who's selling it?
Yeah, but more of what? If nobody wants it, it's just more to store.
I like it, Owen, but I want the plan to include the part where it turns into money.

wobble: Sorry, James, that sounds right. Could the veins come into it somehow?
I'm not sure I know enough to say. Would it need more from the veins, do you think?
That sounds sensible, I think. Though the veins would have to supply it. Sorry.
Sorry, Archie, that makes sense. Could the veins come into it somehow?
I'm not sure I can judge the money. Would it need more from the veins, do you think?
That sounds sensible, I think. The veins would have to bring in the stock, though. Sorry.

james: Buyers pay more for good work, and they come back for it. That's all I'm asking us to be.
I'll grant it takes longer. It also lasts longer, and so does our name.
You may be right about the timing. I'm still right about the work.
archie: Fine, but cash is what lets us fix everything else. Bills first, then the nice stuff.
I hear you. But the bank doesn't take pride, it takes pounds.
Fair point, and I'll watch that. But money's still what keeps the lights on.
owen: Sorry, I know. But it all starts with the veins. If they give more, everything else has more to work with.
You're right, I didn't think about that. I still think it's worth doing, though. If that's all right.
I just think it's the safe bit. We know the veins. We don't have to guess.

james|archie: You'd sell anything someone would pay for, Archie.
Anything decent, and nobody's complained yet. Pride's lovely, James, but I can't pay the rent with it.
The Guild wouldn't put its name on a rushed job for the sake of cash.
The Guild has money behind it. We don't, so I'd like some of that first.
You think every problem is a shortage of money.
Name one that's easier with less of it.
archie|owen: Owen, more yield is great, but the extra's only worth something if we sell it.
Yes, sorry, you're right. I just thought that with more of it, selling would be easier.
You pitch the same thing every time, Owen. Veins, veins, veins.
I know. Sorry. It's what I understand, and I'd rather be right about a small thing than wrong about a big one.
Do you ever want to try a bigger number, Owen?
Sometimes. Then I think about what happens if I'm wrong, and I'd rather not find out.
james|owen: Owen, you can't keep proposing more as if more were an answer.
Sorry, James. It's just that I can see more, and I'm not sure I can see better.
Tell me you'd at least like the work to be good.
I would! I'd just like to be sure there's something to make it from first.
You know the veins better than any of us. Why do you apologise for it?
Habit, I think. Sorry. Sorry about saying sorry.

james: {label}. Good. Now we do it properly.
{label}, then. I'll hold us to the standard.
Sensible choice. {label}, and no corners cut.
archie: Good. {label}. I'll start on it today.
{label}, then. Nice and simple, how I like it.
owen: Oh. {label}? Thank you. I'll do my best.
Really? {label}. Right. I'll get it right, I promise.
{label}, then. Thanks. Sorry, I mean, thank you.

james: Very well. Do it properly, though.
Not what I'd have picked. I'll live.
Acceptable. Don't mistake that for enthusiasm.
archie: Fair enough. Your call. I'll sort the money side.
Not my pick, but fine. We'll see what it brings in.
Go on, then. I'll find a way to make it pay.
owen: Oh, good. I mean, whatever you think is best.
That's all right. I wasn't sure about mine anyway.
Sorry, I'll help however I can.
